content.text: "Anemia or deficiency of hemoglobin is very common in children especially in developing countries. Among the various causes, a poor intake of iron is the commonest reason of this condition and is present in two third of all children. The symptoms are a pale look, irritability and loss of appetite. It is also well known that physical and mental development of these children is affected. Thus it is very important to prevent iron deficiency in children. Milk being a poor source of iron, it is important that child after the six months of age should be given pulses, green vegetables, meats and egg in addition to breast milk", informed Dr Ahmed Naqvi, Consultant Paediatrician, Paediatric Haematologist/Oncologist (blood diseases/cancer) and Assistant Professor of Paediatrics, The Aga Khan University Hospital. He was giving a presentation on "Anemia in Children" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care', monthly health awareness program, held on October 23, 1999.

Dr Naqvi said, ''The other type of anemia commonly seen in Pakistani children is Thalassemia, which results from a genetically determined abnormal hemoglobin. The disease occurs when two genes must be present one from each parent. Thus when both parents are carriers of the abnormal gene (although they do not have severe anemia) there is a 25 percent chance in each pregnancy to have a severely affected baby needing blood transfusion at regular intervals. Intermarriages increase the chance that both parents may carry the gene and thus transmit the disease to their offspring. "

Dr Naqvi added, ''The treatment for this condition is life long blood transfusion usually at four weekly intervals. This leads to excess of iron in the body, which may affect liver, heart, kidneys, brain, etc. To get rid of this iron these children need daily injections of "Desferrioxamine", which is given under the skin by a pump over a 8 - 12 hour period (during night). The other treatment for this condition is bone marrow transplantation but unfortunately this is not available in Pakistan. Therefore, the best hope for our country is prevention of this disease."

Dr Naqvi concluded by saying that in communities where Thalassemia is commonly seen, all children and young adults should be screened by doing a simple blood test. If they are carrying the disease then all efforts should be made that such a person should not marry the other carrying the same gene. For couples who have a child with Thalassemia, antenatal diagnosis is available at centres including AKUH. For patients with Thalassemia, it is important to receive regular, screened blood transfusions. In addition they should also receive the iron removing medicine "Desferrioxamine" regularly. These children should also get Hepatitis B vaccination at the earliest possible. The life span of these children with irregular transfusions and no treatment for removing excess iron from their bodies, is usually 10 - 15 years. But with the above measures, i.e. regular blood transfusions and excess iron removal, these children can be expected a normal life of usual longevity."
